metadata.title: Claude, Escalation Flagger.
metadata.purpose: Answer whether a Claude Skill named escalation-flagger flags things by Claude's own judgment about what looks risky, or by a match against criteria written down in a file -- using the general mechanism every Claude Skill shares (a folder, one SKILL.md, criteria checked in order) since the source never states escalation-flagger's specific criteria or escalation target. Lands the carry-out that a flag is a match against a written file, not a judgment call: reliable inside what's written, silent past its edge.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B03 (the SKILL.md card with its numbered checklist of criteria, run twice with identical match-and-flag results, then a case outside the file with nothing to match)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes escalation-flagger decides what's risky using its own judgment. It doesn't. It matches input against criteria written in SKILL.md. So — is it flagging by judgment, or by match?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude's escalation flagger — is it flagging things it thinks are risky?', hesitates on 'thinks', corrects to 'matches', lands the real question

props.text:

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('thinks' -> 'matches') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A Claude Skill is just a folder Claude reads before it works. This one is named escalation-flagger, and everything it knows lives in one file: SKILL.md — plain sentences, not code. Open it, and you'd see something like a numbered list of criteria, checked one after another. Claude reads that file, then follows it. The file decides what gets flagged, not Claude.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — a SKILL.md card opening, a numbered checklist of criteria

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — SKILL.md, a numbered checklist
production_viz.mechanic: A folder labeled escalation-flagger opens into a SKILL.md card. A numbered checklist of criteria types itself in top to bottom, one lighting up with a checkmark. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: It can look like Claude is sensing which things feel risky — that's the guess most people make. It isn't. Claude checks each item on the list, one criterion after another, and flags only where one actually matches. Remove a criterion from that file, and inputs that used to trigger it stop being flagged. Nothing hidden fills the gap.

shot.new_visual_element: The wrong guess, drawn then struck; the checklist mechanism

production_viz.label: Checked, not sensed
production_viz.mechanic: An input checked against a linear list of criteria, one item at a time; one criterion struck out in terracotta; the same input then passes through afterward with no flag.

beats.narration_text: Go back to that same SKILL.md and its list of criteria. Run the same input through escalation-flagger twice, and you get the same match and the same flag both times — for as long as the input matches something written there. Send through a case the list never anticipated, and nothing gets flagged — not because Claude judged it safe, but because nothing in the file matched it.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same SKILL.md card, run twice, then a case with nothing to match

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same match, then no match
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01 COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical — the same SKILL.md card, run twice side by side, the same criterion lit both times. Then a new input shape passes down the list with no matching criterion and exits unflagged.

beats.narration_text: A flag isn't Claude's judgment call — it's a match against criteria written in a file. Same match, same flag, every time; no match, no flag, however it looks to a person.

props.quote: A flag isn't Claude's judgment call — it's a match against criteria written in a file. Same match, same flag, every time; no match, no flag, however it looks to a person.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me: write me a SKILL.md with three short numbered criteria for flagging something you deal with often. Then hand it inputs on both sides — one that matches, one that doesn't — and watch whether the flag follows the file, not a feeling. Liam, in for Bear.
